Report Local Quill

1 Introduction

Automated writing feedback has become increasingly accessible through large language models (LLMs); however, most solutions depend on cloud-hosted models from tech companies. This raises concerns around data privacy. For students submitting coursework and young authors developing unpublished work, there is a meaningful risk that submitted text may be retained or used for model training by third-party providers. This creates a need for a locally deployable feedback system which keeps all user data on-device.

Local Quill targets this gap. The project focuses on two writing categories: academic essays and fictional prose. Both are reflective of the two primary user groups in need of targeted feedback: students who require structured feedback and aspiring authors seeking narrative and stylistic guidance. The goal is to deliver feedback reflective of the category using only local models within the scope of user hardware.

Local deployment naturally favours small-parameter LLMs of approximately 8 billion parameters, which is reflected in the size of context windows, reduced instruction-following capacity and degraded output quality on open-ended tasks. However this is precisely a task type where retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) shines. A high-quality pipeline of publicly available writing guides and style manuals was selected to build a focused knowledge base. A context is retrieved and injected into the system prompt on every query to ground model answers with field-specific knowledge and ensure high-quality responses.

Feedback generation is further structured into three focused sub-tasks: grammar, clarity and style, each handled through a separate LLM prompt. This decomposition allows each call to specialise in a single dimension, producing more targeted feedback than a single composite prompt could.

The research question of the project is: Can a local solution within the scope of 8b-parameter LLM models achieve results comparable to GPT-5-nano, given the context provided by RAG writing guidelines, as measured by G-Eval metrics?

The remainder of the report is structured as follows. Section 2 State of the Art reviews LLM structure and compression as well as RAG techniques. The section 3 Data describes the writing guidelines and test data used in the RAG pipeline. The section 4 Methods focuses on the steps taken during development. The environment setup through prompt engineering, RAG pipeline and G-Eval. The section 5 Results analyses the G-Eval results for embedding and LLM models. Finally, the section 6 Conclusions discusses the results and proposes further development.

2 State of the Art

2.1 Large Language Models

Research institutes have generated text and images for decades, but the release of Attention Is All You Need [1] in 2017 marked a turning point. The transformer architecture contained both encoder and decoder architectures, which were regulated through self-attention. For text generation, it allowed models to weigh the relevance of every previous word when producing the next. This enabled a qualitative improvement in text coherence and the understanding of context over prior recurrent neural network approaches.

These transformer models were developed and scaled by research labs over the following years, but public attention peaked in 2022 with the release of ChatGPT. Its conversational interface made the technology accessible to average users for the first time, which triggered widespread adoption across writing, coding, and education.

Training a full LLM from scratch requires vast computational resources and task-specific data at a scale far beyond student projects, even for most smaller companies. However, there are countless pretrained transformer models perfectly suited for zero-shot generalization tasks. This architecture is known as Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT). Unfortunately the most capable models contain billions of parameters and are only accessible via the cloud, which is precisely the constraint this project addresses.

2.2 Model Compression

This introduces major privacy concerns; powerful models capable of generating feedback exist, but using them means potentially exposing user data. This requires a local alternative. Fortunately, powerful models can compress their knowledge base to create compact models with only a few billion parameters.

"Quantization (Gray and Neuhoff, 1998) refers to the process of reducing the number of bits (i.e., precision) in the parameters of the model with minimal loss in inference performance." [2] With two distinct variations: quantization-aware training, which retrains a quantized model to counteract performance degradation, while post-training quantization directly converts a full LLM.

This quantization method is used on various powerful LLM models, and countless compressed models exist. Many remain in the hands of powerful companies; however, there are publicly available open-source models for companies and private users. Some companies share their smaller models to encourage further development. There are multiple websites which serve this purpose. This privacy can be guaranteed since every query is executed on the same machine, and the models can be checked since they have to be downloaded from Ollama in the compressed GGUF format. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that injects targeted context at query time. For this purpose, the user prompt needs to be encoded for a similarity search to be performed on a vector database consisting of external files. Since the context is selected from previously prepared documents, the accuracy of responses can be greatly enhanced. Forgetting information and updating it regularly is a known issue with RAG systems; however, this project ages slowly since writing and style guides only change at the pace of natural languages.

‘I remember it as if it were yesterday that my English teacher came to me during a school break and asked me, “How would you like to go to Canada for a month to study at a local high school, all expenses paid?” As you can imagine, my jaw dropped something like ten feet at the mere thought of it. I was sixteen at the time, and it seemed like the world was opening in front of me. After I recovered from the immediate shock, I said I would go in a heartbeat, and so we went into the Principal’s office to call my mother. It wasn’t me making the phone call, but I could perfectly imagine what my mum’s face was at the other end of the line. First of all, she would be completely puzzled that I was at the Principal’s office because I never get into trouble. Secondly, after that, I imagine she was in utter disbelief when she heard the words: “your daughter is going to Canada for a month, if that is okay with you of course.” They passed me the phone and my mum asked me: “Do you want to go?” to which I said: “YES!” And that was it, my future had taken a new direction and I was going to be in Canada by the end of the year.
As I had expected I made a lot of new friends, I fell in love with all the members of the family that took me in, and I was completely blown away by their completely different way of life.
It is funny though how, despite having had all those wonderful experiences once I got there, I sometimes find myself thinking about the time I was told that, if I wanted it, the opportunity was mine, rather than about the time I spent in the actual country.
I believe that recalling memorable events in our lives has a very positive effect on us. It makes us feel special, it makes us think back on halcyon times and that joy spreads and is contagious. Suddenly we find ourselves feeling that happiness in every fibre of our beings.

A high-quality pipeline of publicly available writing guides and style manuals was selected to build a focused knowledge base. A context is retrieved and injected into the system prompt on every query to ground model answers with field-specific knowledge and ensure high-quality responses.

Feedback generation is further structured into three focused sub-tasks: grammar, clarity and style, each handled though a separate LLM prompt. This decomposition allows each call to specialise in a single dimension, producing more targeted feedback than a single composite prompt could.

The research question of the project is: Can a local solution within the scope of 8b-parameter LLM models achieve results comparable to GPT-5-nano, given the context provided by RAG writing guidelines, as measured by G-Eval metrics?

The remainder of the report is structured as follows. Section 2 State of the Art reviews LLM structure and compression as well as RAG techniques. Section 3 Data describes the writing guidelines and test data used in the RAG pipeline. Section 4 Methods focuses on the steps taken during development: the environment setup through prompt engineering, RAG pipeline and G-Eval. Section 5 Results analyses the G-Eval results for embedding and LLM models. Finally, Section 6 Conclusions discusses the results and proposes further development.

2 State of the Art

2.1 Large Language Models

Research institutes have generated text and images for decades, but the release of Attention Is All You Need [1] in 2017 marked a turning point. The transformer architecture contains both encoder and decoder architectures, which are regulated through self-attention. For text generation, it allowed models to weigh the relevance of every previous word when producing the next. This enabled a qualitative improvement in text coherence and the understanding of context over prior recurrent neural network approaches.

These transformer models were developed and scaled by research labs over the following years, but public attention peaked in 2022 with the release of ChatGPT. Its conversational interface made the technology accessible to average users for the first time, which triggered widespread adoption across writing, coding, and education.

Training a full LLM from scratch requires vast computational resources and task-specific data at a scale far beyond student projects, even for most smaller companies. However, there are countless pretrained transformer models perfectly suited for zero-shot generalisation tasks. This architecture is known as Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT). Unfortunately the most capable models contain billions of parameters and are only accessible via the cloud, which is precisely the constraint this project addresses.

2.2 Model Compression

This introduces major privacy concerns; powerful models capable of generating feedback exist, but using them means potentially exposing user data. This requires a local alternative. Fortunately, powerful models can compress their knowledge base to create compact models with only a few billion parameters.

"Quantisation (Gray and Neuhoff, 1998) refers to the process of reducing the number of bits (i.e., precision) in the parameters of the model with minimal loss in inference performance." [2] With two distinct variations: quantisation-aware training, which retrains a quantised model to counteract performance degradation, while post-training quantisation directly converts a full LLM.

This quantisation method is used on various powerful LLM models, and countless compressed models exist. Many remain in the hands of powerful companies; however, there are publicly available open-source models for companies and private users. These models include 8‑billion parameter models, which can be self-hosted on a local machine. The perfect sweet spot between privacy and model power. The only remaining issue is the model source.

2.3 Ollama

Some companies share their smaller models to encourage further development. There are multiple websites which serve this purpose. From the widely open-source Hugging Face, to Ollama, owned by Llamafactory. However, Ollama offers a runtime for locally hosted quantised models without requiring a connection, which suited this project better. On the other hand, Ollama models also arrive with hardware requirements and performance limitations. This limitation primarily affects query speed in return for absolute privacy.

This privacy can be guaranteed since every query is executed on the same machine, and the models can be checked since they have to be downloaded from Ollama in the compressed GGUF format. GGUF is "[...]a binary format that is optimised for quick loading and saving of models, making it highly efficient for inference purposes." [3]

Thus, a compressed model is downloaded over the Ollama site and can be targeted via local API calls. Only the response quality of compressed LLMs remains a severe issue, since compression always comes at a trade-off.

2.4 Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that injects targeted context at query time. For this purpose, the user prompt needs to be encoded for a similarity search to be performed on a vector database consisting of external files. These files are predominantly used to build a knowledge base backend to supplement compressed LLMs by retrieving task-specific information. [4]

The use case in these projects differs slightly, since guidelines are retrieved in contrast to the more traditional information retrieval [5], which requires more reasoning from the quantised models than simply returning information.

A metaparameter determines the number of similar vectors the similarity search returns, which are then decoded back into chunks before prompting the LLM. Since the context is selected from previously prepared documents, the accuracy of responses can be greatly enhanced. This allows even compact models to achieve significantly better results if the task is specific enough and the documents are not yet outdated.

Forgetting information and updating it regularly is a known issue with RAG systems; however, this project ages slowly since writing and style guides only change at the pace of natural languages.

3 Data

The knowledge base comprises 12 PDF documents, a total of 17 MB, drawn from three categories: essay writing guides, fiction writing guides, and test materials. All sources are publicly available resources from academic institutions and educational platforms, written predominantly in UK English. No personally identifiable information is present in any document. Table 1 gives a full overview.

Essay writing sources cover argument structure, essay structure, vocabulary, and clarity. Fiction writing sources address narrative style, point of view, dialogue formatting, and idiomatic language. Test materials consist of Cambridge English sample responses across CEFR levels A1-C2, an accompanying assessment guide, and an excerpt from Chapter 1 of The Fellowship of the Ring, used solely for fiction evaluation.

A book that brings back endless memories of my childhood is The Hobbit by J. R. R. Tolkien. This story is a prequel to the trilogy The Lord of the Rings and narrates the life of an extraordinary dwarf named Bilbo Baggins.

The reason why this book has a special place in my heart is because of the euphoria and excitement it brought when I was flipping through the pages as a kid after reading.

The story is based on an adventure that Bilbo Baggins undergoes after being persuaded by an eccentric wizard called Gandalf to join him and the other dwarves.

Bilbo's life takes a quick turn—from living in a Hobbit-hole to battling bizarre creatures and monsters in the woods.

The story had more intense moments that, as a child, left me completely hooked on the plot.

The ultimate goal of the protagonist was to defeat the malevolent and sinister dragon called Smaug and reclaim all of the gold that he stole from the dwarves.

Even up to this day I still consider Bilbo Baggins one of the most heroic fictional characters of all time. He was a normal man living a normal and ordinary life before he transformed into the benevolent man that made the most heart-touching and ecstatic memories in this plot.

The impact this book has on me was colossal. I learnt so much—a great deal of values and ethics from all the characters that made a worthwhile contribution to the story—from learning to remain humble to respecting your kin and mustering the courage to take up any challenge, no matter how difficult it may seem. I would also venture to say that this book, although classical, remains highly relevant for youth in upcoming generations, not only because of the valuable lessons it has to offer, but also because of the mixed feelings of melancholy, merriment, bafflement and adrenaline rushes you may experience while reading.

Lorries need to travel at full speed to carry the necessary materials for the construction. People whose workplaces are located in the centre have no choice but to drive through our town to their work every day. Therefore, our town, which used to be quiet and peaceful, has become noisier. Last but not least, people should be shown alternative routes that lead to the centre so that they do not put pressure on our infrastructure. 

I hope that my complaint can be taken into consideration so that our town can become an enjoyable place to live again.

'An Unforgettable Event'
I remember it as if it were yesterday when my English teacher came to me during a school break and asked me, 'How would you like to go to Canada for a month to study at a local high school, all expenses paid?' As you can imagine, my jaw dropped about ten feet at the mere thought of it.

I was sixteen at the time, and it seemed as if the world was opening before me.

After I had recovered from the immediate shock, I said I would go in a heartbeat, and so we went to the Principal's office to call my mother.

It wasn't me making the phone call, but I could perfectly imagine what my mum's face would be at the other end of the line.

First of all, she would be completely puzzled that I was at the Principal's office because I never got into trouble.

Secondly, after that, I imagined she would be in utter disbelief when she heard the words: 'Your daughter is going to Canada for a month, if that is okay with you, of course.'

They passed me the phone and my mum asked me, 'Do you want to go?' to which I said, 'Yes!'

And that was it; my future had taken a new direction and I was going to be in Canada by the end of the year.

As I had expected, I made a lot of new friends; I fell in love with all the members of the family that took me in, and I was completely blown away by their completely different way of life.

It is funny, though, how, despite having had all those wonderful experiences once I got there, I sometimes find myself thinking about the time I was told that, if I wanted to, the opportunity was mine, rather than about the time I spent in the actual country.

I believe that recalling memorable events in our lives has a very positive effect on us. It makes us feel special; it makes us think back on halcyon times and that joy spreads and it is contagious. Suddenly we find ourselves feeling that happiness in every fibre of our being.

It is an undeniable truth that technology has become a mainstay in our lives. From our personal lives to our public sphere tasks, there is a perpetual flow of gadgets and gizmos creeping into our environments to assist us with our activities. And what's not to like? For the most part, even the most monotonous of tasks have become quicker and easier with the help of these inventions.

Of course, there are those who are not yet completely comfortable with this notion. The sheer acceleration with which new technologies are brought to life is enough to make any tradition-oriented person run for the hills! In fact, there are studies in which it has been proven that an individual's ability to cope with this phenomenon mirrors their character. People who hold tighter reins on the happenings in their lives tend to welcome the change, whereas those who are less confident see it as a threat to a certain degree.

This leads to an impasse in the workplace; an employee probably cannot avoid working with new technology altogether at first, simply because they are less confident. Therefore it is imperative that workers are effective and practically trained so that they can be in control, and thus have no qualms about new innovations. The first step here would be to instill the right mindset in employees by assuring them that they will gain greatly from this change. In fact, this is a vital step in any effort to seamlessly integrate humans and technology, as it paves the way for far greater developments in the future.

TEXT:
"""
Report Local Quill

1 Introduction

Automated writing feedback has become increasingly accessible through large language models (LLMs); however, most solutions depend on cloud-hosted models from tech companies. This raises concerns around data privacy. For students submitting coursework and young authors developing unpublished work, there is a meaningful risk that submitted text may be retained or used for model training by third-party providers. This creates a need for a locally deployable feedback system that keeps all user data on-device.

Local Quill targets this gap. The project focuses on two writing categories: academic essays and fictional prose. Both are reflective of the two primary user groups in need of targeted feedback: students who require structured feedback and aspiring authors seeking narrative and stylistic guidance. The goal is to deliver feedback that reflects the category, using only local models within the scope of user hardware.

Local deployment naturally favours small-parameter LLMs of approximately 8 billion parameters, which is reflected in the size of context windows, reduced instruction-following capacity, and degraded output quality on open-ended tasks. However, this is precisely a task type where retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) shines. A high-quality pipeline of publicly available writing guides and style manuals was selected to build a focused knowledge base. A context is retrieved and injected into the system prompt for every query to ground model answers with field-specific knowledge and ensure high-quality responses.

Feedback generation is structured into three focused sub-tasks: grammar, clarity, and style, each handled through a separate LLM prompt. This decomposition allows each call to specialise in a single dimension, producing more targeted feedback than a single composite prompt could.

The research question of the project is: Can a local solution within the scope of 8b-parameter LLM models achieve results comparable to GPT-5-nano, given the context provided by RAG writing guidelines, as measured by G-Eval metrics?

The remainder of the report is structured as follows. Section 2 State of the Art reviews LLM structure and compression as well as RAG techniques. Section 3 Data describes the writing guidelines and test data used in the RAG pipeline. Section 4 Methods focuses on the steps taken during development. The environment setup through prompt engineering, RAG pipeline and G-Eval. Section 5 Results analyse the G-Eval results for embedding and LLM models. Finally, Section 6 Conclusions discusses the results and proposes further development.

2 State of the Art

2.1 Large Language Models

Research institutes have generated text and images for decades, but the release of Attention Is All You Need [1] in 2017 marked a turning point. The transformer architecture contained both encoder and decoder components, which were enabled by self-attention. For text generation, it allowed models to weigh the relevance of every previous word when producing the next word. This enabled a qualitative improvement in text coherence and the understanding of context over prior recurrent neural network approaches.

These transformer models were developed and scaled by research labs over the following years, but public attention peaked in 2022 with the release of ChatGPT. Its conversational interface made the technology accessible to average users for the first time, which triggered widespread adoption across writing, coding, and education.

Training a full LLM from scratch requires vast computational resources and task-specific data at a scale far beyond student projects, even for most smaller companies. However, there are countless pretrained transformer models perfectly suited for zero-shot generalisation tasks. This architecture is known as Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT). Unfortunately the most capable models contain billions of parameters and are only accessible via the cloud, which is precisely the constraint this project addresses.

2.2 Model Compression

This introduces major privacy concerns; powerful models capable of generating feedback exist, but using them means potentially exposing user data. This requires a local alternative. Fortunately, powerful models can compress their knowledge base to create compact models with only a few billion parameters.

"Quantisation (Gray and Neuhoff, 1998) refers to the process of reducing the number of bits (i.e., precision) in the parameters of the model with minimal loss in inference performance." [2] There are two distinct variations: quantisation-aware training, which retrains a quantised model to counteract performance degradation, and post-training quantisation, which directly converts a full LLM.

This quantisation method is used on various powerful LLMs, and countless compressed models exist. Many remain in the hands of powerful companies; however, there are publicly available open-source models for companies and private users. These models include 8‑billion-parameter models, which can be self-hosted on a local machine. They represent the perfect sweet spot between privacy and model power. The only remaining issue is the model source.

2.3 Ollama

Some companies share their smaller models to encourage further development. There are multiple websites that serve this purpose. From the widely open-source Hugging Face to Ollama, owned by Llamafactory. However, Ollama offers a runtime for locally hosted quantised models without requiring a connection, which suited this project better. On the other hand, Ollama models also arrive with hardware requirements and performance limitations. This limitation is primarily affecting query speed in return for absolute privacy.

This privacy can be guaranteed since every query is executed on the same machine, and the models can be checked since they have to be downloaded from Ollama in the compressed GGUF format. GGUF is "[...]a binary format that is optimised for quick loading and saving of models, making it highly efficient for inference purposes." [3]

Thus, a compressed model is downloaded from the Ollama site and can be targeted via local API calls. Only the response quality of compressed LLMs remains a severe issue, since compression always comes at a trade-off.

2.4 Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that injects targeted context at query time. For this purpose, the user prompt needs to be encoded so that a similarity search can be performed on a vector database consisting of external files. These files are predominantly used to build a knowledge-base backend to supplement compressed LLMs by retrieving task-specific information. [4]

The use case in these projects differs slightly, since guidelines are retrieved in contrast to the more traditional information retrieval [5], which requires more reasoning from the quantised models than simply returning information.

A metaparameter determines the number of similar vectors that the similarity search returns, which are then decoded back into chunks before prompting the LLM. Since the context is selected from previously prepared documents, the accuracy of responses can be greatly enhanced. This allows even compact models to achieve significantly better results if the task is specific enough and the documents are not yet outdated.

Forgetting information and updating it regularly is a known issue with RAG systems; however, this project ages slowly since writing and style guides change only at the pace of natural language.

3 Data

The knowledge base comprises 12 PDF documents, a total of 17 MB, drawn from three categories: essay writing guides, fiction writing guides, and test materials. All sources are publicly available resources from academic institutions and educational platforms, written predominantly in UK English. No personally identifiable information is present in any document. Table 1 gives a full overview.

Essay writing sources cover argument structure, essay structure, vocabulary, and clarity. Fiction writing sources address narrative style, point of view, dialogue formatting, and idiomatic language. Test materials consist of Cambridge English sample responses across CEFR levels A1–C2, an accompanying assessment guide, and an excerpt from Chapter 1 of The Fellowship of the Ring, used solely for fiction evaluation.

"""

output:
Report Local Quill

1 Introduction

Automated writing feedback has become increasingly accessible through large language models (LLMs); however, most solutions depend on cloud-hosted models from tech companies. This raises concerns around data privacy. For students submitting coursework and young authors developing unpublished work, there is a meaningful risk that submitted text may be retained or used for model training by third-party providers. This creates a need for a locally deployable feedback system which keeps all user data on-device.

Local Quill targets this gap. The project focuses on two writing categories: academic essays and fictional prose. Both are reflective of the two primary user groups in need of targeted feedback: students who require structured feedback and aspiring authors seeking narrative and stylistic guidance. The goal is to deliver feedback reflective of the category using only local models within the scope of user hardware.

Local deployment naturally favours small-parameter LLMs of approximately 8 billion parameters, which is reflected in the size of context windows, reduced instruction-following capacity and degraded output quality on open-ended tasks. However, this is precisely a task type where retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) shines. A high-quality pipeline of publicly available writing guides and style manuals was selected to build a focused knowledge base. A context is retrieved and injected into the system prompt on every query to ground model answers with field-specific knowledge and ensure high-quality responses.

Feedback generation is further structured into three focused sub-tasks: grammar, clarity and style, each handled through a separate LLM prompt. This decomposition allows each call to specialise in a single dimension, producing more targeted feedback than a single composite prompt could.

The research question of the project is: Can a local solution within the scope of 8b-parameter LLM models achieve results comparable to GPT-5-nano, given the context provided by RAG writing guidelines, as measured by G-Eval metrics?

The remainder of the report is structured as follows. Section 2 State of the Art reviews LLM structure and compression as well as RAG techniques. Section 3 Data describes the writing guidelines and test data used in the RAG pipeline. Section 4 Methods focuses on the steps taken during development. The environment setup through prompt engineering, RAG pipeline and G-Eval. The section 5 Results analyses the G-Eval results for embedding and LLM models. Finally, the section 6 Conclusions discusses the results and proposes further development.

2 State of the Art

2.1 Large Language Models

Research institutes have generated text and images for decades, but the release of Attention Is All You Need in 2017 marked a turning point. The transformer architecture contains both encoder and decoder architectures, which are governed by self-attention. For text generation, it allowed models to weigh the relevance of every previous word in order to produce the next. This enabled a qualitative improvement in text coherence and the understanding of context over prior recurrent neural network approaches.

These transformer models were developed and scaled by research labs over the following years, but public attention peaked in 2022 with the release of ChatGPT. Its conversational interface made the technology accessible to average users for the first time, which triggered widespread adoption across writing, coding, and education.

Training a full LLM from scratch requires vast computational resources and task-specific data at a scale far beyond student projects, even for most smaller companies. However, there are countless pretrained transformer models perfectly suited for zero-shot generalization tasks. This architecture is known as Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT). Unfortunately the most capable models contain billions of parameters and are only accessible via the cloud, which is precisely the constraint this project addresses.

2.2 Model Compression

This introduces major privacy concerns; powerful models capable of generating feedback exist, but using them means potentially exposing user data. This requires a local alternative. Fortunately, powerful models can compress their knowledge base to create compact models with only a few billion parameters.

"Quantization (Gray and Neuhoff, 1998) refers to the process of reducing the number of bits (i.e., precision) in the parameters of the model, with minimal loss in inference performance." There are two distinct variations: quantisation-aware training, which retrains a quantised model to counteract performance degradation, and post-quantisation, which directly converts a full LLM.

This quantisation method is used on various powerful LLM models, and countless compressed models exist. Many remain in the hands of powerful companies; however, there are publicly available open-source models for organisations and private users. These models include 8‑billion parameter models, which can be self-hosted on a local machine. The perfect sweet spot between privacy and model power. The only remaining issue is the model source.

2.3 Ollama

Some companies share their smaller models to encourage further development. There are multiple websites which serve this purpose. From the widely open-source Hugging Face, to Ollama, owned by Llamafactory. However, Ollama offers a runtime for locally hosted quantized models without requiring a connection, which suited this project better. On the other hand, Ollama models also arrive with hardware requirements and performance limitations. This limitation primarily affects query speed in return for absolute privacy.

This privacy can be guaranteed since every query is executed on the same machine, and the models can be checked since they have to be downloaded from Ollama in the compressed GGUF format. GGUF is "a binary format that is optimised for quick loading and saving of models, making it highly efficient for inference purposes." [3]

Thus, a compressed model is downloaded over the Ollama site and can be targeted via local API calls. Only the response quality of compressed LLMs remains a severe issue, since compression always comes at a trade-off.

2.4 Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that injects targeted context at query time. For this purpose, the user prompt needs to be encoded for a similarity search to be performed on a vector database consisting of external files. These files are predominantly used to build a knowledge-base backend to supplement compressed LLMs by retrieving task-specific information. [4]

The use case in these projects differs slightly, since guidelines are retrieved, in contrast to the more traditional information retrieval, which requires more reasoning from the quantised models than simply returning information. [5]

A metaparameter determines the number of similar vectors that the similarity search returns, which are then decoded back into chunks before prompting the LLM. Since the context is selected from previously prepared documents, the accuracy of responses can be greatly enhanced. This allows even compact models to achieve significantly better results if the task is specific enough and the documents are not yet outdated.

Forgetting information and updating it regularly is a known issue with RAG systems; however, this project ages slowly since writing and style guides change only at the pace of natural language.

3 Data

The knowledge base comprises 12 PDF documents, a total of 17 MB, drawn from three categories: essay writing guides, fiction writing guides, and test materials. All sources are publicly available resources from academic institutions and educational platforms, written predominantly in UK English. No personal identifiable information is present in any document. Table 1 gives a full overview.

Essay writing sources cover argument structure, essay structure, vocabulary, and clarity. Fiction writing sources address narrative style, point of view, dialogue formatting, and idiomatic language. Test materials consist of Cambridge English sample responses across CEFR levels A1–C2, an accompanying assessment guide, and an excerpt from Chapter 1 of The Fellowship of the Ring, used solely for fiction evaluation.

A book that brings endless memory of my childhood is “The Hobbit” by J. R. R Tolkien. This story is a prequel to the trilogy “The Lord of The Rings” and narrates the life of an extraordinary dwarf named Bilbo Baggins.

The reason this book has a special place in my heart is because of the euphoria and excitement it brought as I was flipping through the pages as a kid after reading. The story is based on an adventure that Bilbo Baggins undergoes after being persuaded by a eccentric wizard called Gandalf to joining him and other dwarfs. Bilbo's life takes a quick turn – from living in a “Hobbit Hole” to battling bizarre creatures and monsters in the woods. The story had many intense moments that, as a child, left me completely hooked on the plot.

The ultimate goal of the protagonist was to defeat a malevolent and sinister dragon called “Smaug” and reclaim all of the gold that he stole from the dwarves. Even up to this day I still consider Bilbo Baggins one of the most heroic fictional characters of all time. He was a normal man living a normal and ordinary life before he transformed into the benevolent man who made the most heart-touching and ecstatic memories in this plot.

The impact this book has on me is colossal. I learned a great deal of values and ethics from all the characters that made a worthwhile contribution to the story – from learning to remain humble to respecting your kins and mustering the courage to take up any challenge, no matter how difficult it may seem. I would also venture to say that this book, although classical, remains highly relevant for the youth in upcoming generations, not only because of the valuable lesson it has to offer, but because of the mixed feelings of melancholy, merriness, bafflement and adrenaline rushes you may experience while reading.

‘An Unforgettable Event’
I remember it as if it were yesterday when my English teacher came to me during a school break and asked me: ‘How would you like to go to Canda Canada for a month to study at a local highschoo high school, all expenses paid?’ As you can imagine, my jaw dropped something like ten feet at the mere thought of it. I was sixteen at the time, and it seemed like the world was opening in front of me. After I recovered from the immediate shock, I said I would go in a heartbeat, and so we went into the Principal’s office to call my mother. It wasn't me making the phone call, but I could perfectly imagine what my mom’s face was at the other end of the line. First of all, she would be completely puzzled that I was at the Principal’s office because I never get into trouble. Secondly, after that, I imagine she was in utter disbelief when she heard the words: ‘your daughter is going to Canada for a month, if that is okay with you, of course.’ They passed me the phone and my mum asked me: ‘Do you want to go?’ to which I said: ‘YES!’ And that was it; my future had taken a new direction, and I was going to be in Canada by the end of the year.
As I had expected, I made a lot of new friends; I fell in love with all the members of the family who took me in, and I was completely blown away by their completely different way of life.
It is funny, though, how, despite having had all those wonderful experiences once I got there, I sometimes find myself thinking about the time I was told that, if I wanted to, the opportunity was mine, rather than about the time I spent in the actual country.
I believe that recalling memorable events in our lives has a very positive effect on us. It makes us feel special; it makes us think back on halcyon times and that joy spreads, and it is contagious. Suddenly we find ourselves feeling that happiness in every fibre of our beings.

From our personal lives to our public sphere tasks there is a perpetual flow of gadgets and gizmos creeping into our environments to assist us with our activities. And what's not to like? The first step here would be to instill the right mindset in employees by assuring them that they will gain greatly from this change. In fact, this is a vital step in any effort to seamlessly integrate humans and technology, as it paves the way for far greater developments in the future.

TEXT:
"""
Report Local Quill

1 Introduction

Automated writing feedback has become increasingly accessible through large language models (LLMs); however, most solutions depend on cloud-hosted models from tech companies. This raises concerns about data privacy. For students submitting coursework and young authors developing unpublished work, there is a meaningful risk that submitted text may be retained or used for model training by third-party providers. This creates a need for a locally deployable feedback system that keeps all user data on-device.

Local Quill targets this gap. The project focuses on two writing categories: academic essays and fictional prose. Both are reflective of the two primary user groups in need of targeted feedback: students who require structured feedback and aspiring authors seeking narrative and stylistic guidance. The goal is to deliver feedback reflective of the category using only local models within the scope of the user's hardware.

Local deployment naturally favours small-parameter LLMs of approximately 8 billion parameters, which are reflected in the size of context windows, reduced instruction-following capacity, and degraded output quality on open-ended tasks. However, this is precisely a task type where Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) shines. A high-quality pipeline of publicly available writing guides and style manuals was selected to build a focused knowledge base. A context is retrieved and injected into the system prompt on every query to ground the model's answers with field-specific knowledge and ensure high-quality responses.

Feedback generation is further structured into three focused sub-tasks: grammar, clarity and style, each handled through a separate LLM prompt. This decomposition allows each call to specialise in a single dimension, producing more targeted feedback than a single composite prompt could.

The research question of the project is: Can a local solution within the scope of 8‑billion-parameter LLM models achieve results comparable to GPT-5-nano, given the context provided by RAG writing guidelines, as measured by G-Eval metrics?

The remainder of the report is structured as follows. Section 2 State of the Art reviews LLM structure and compression as well as RAG techniques. The section 3 Data describes the writing guidelines and test data used in the RAG pipeline. The section 4 Methods focuses on the steps taken during development. The environment setup through prompt engineering, RAG pipeline and G-Eval. The section 5 Results analyses the G-Eval results for embedding and LLM models. Finally, the section 6 Conclusions discusses the results and proposes further development.

2 State of the Art

2.1 Large Language Models

Research institutes have generated text and images for decades, but the release of Attention Is All You Need [1] in 2017 marked a turning point. The Transformer architecture contains both encoder and decoder components, which are regulated by self-attention. For text generation, it allowed models to weigh the relevance of every previous word when producing the next. This enabled a qualitative improvement in text coherence and the understanding of context over prior recurrent neural network approaches.

These Transformer models were developed and scaled by research labs in the following years, but public attention peaked in 2022 with the release of ChatGPT. Its conversational interface made the technology accessible to the average user for the first time, which triggered widespread adoption across writing, coding, and education.

Training a full LLM from scratch requires vast computational resources and task-specific data at a scale far beyond that of student projects, even for most smaller companies. However, there are countless pretrained transformer models perfectly suited for zero-shot generalisation tasks. This architecture is known as Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPT). Unfortunately the most capable models contain billions of parameters and are only accessible via the cloud, which is precisely the constraint this project addresses.

2.2 Model Compression

This introduces major privacy concerns; powerful models capable of generating feedback exist, but using them means potentially exposing user data. This requires a local alternative. Fortunately, powerful models can compress their knowledge base to create compact models with only a few billion parameters.

Quantisation (Gray and Neuhoff, 1998) refers to the process of reducing the number of bits (i.e., precision) in the parameters of the model with minimal loss in inference performance [2]. There are two distinct variations: quantisation-aware training, which retrains a quantised model to counteract performance degradation, and post-training quantisation, which directly converts a full LLM.

This quantisation method is used on various powerful LLMs, and countless compressed models exist. Many remain in the hands of powerful companies; however, there are publicly available open-source models for companies and private users. These models include 8‑billion-parameter models, which can be self-hosted on a local machine. This represents the perfect sweet spot between privacy and model power. The only remaining issue is the model source.

2.3 Ollama

Some companies share their smaller models to encourage further development. There are multiple websites that serve this purpose, from Hugging Face, the widely used open-source platform, to Ollama, owned by Llamafactory. However, Ollama offers a runtime for locally hosted quantised models without requiring a connection, which suits this project better. On the other hand, Ollama models also arrive with hardware requirements and performance limitations. This limitation primarily affects query speed in return for absolute privacy.

This privacy can be guaranteed since every query is executed on the same machine, and the models can be verified because they are downloaded from Ollama in the compressed GGUF format. GGUF is a binary format that is optimised for quick loading and saving of models, making it highly efficient for inference purposes [3].

Thus, a compressed model is downloaded from the Ollama site and can be targeted via local API calls. Only the response quality of compressed LLMs remains a severe issue, since compression always comes at a trade-off.

2.4 Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that injects targeted context at query time. For this purpose, the user prompt must be encoded so that a similarity search can be performed on a vector database consisting of external files. These files are predominantly used to build a knowledge-base backend to supplement compressed LLMs by retrieving task-specific information. [4]

The use case in these projects differs slightly, since guidelines are retrieved rather than simply returning information; this contrasts with traditional information retrieval [5], which requires more reasoning from the quantised models than merely returning information.

A metaparameter determines the number of similar vectors the similarity search returns, which are then decoded back into chunks before prompting the LLM. Since the context is selected from previously prepared documents, the accuracy of responses can be greatly enhanced. This allows even compact models to achieve significantly better results if the task is specific enough and the documents are not yet outdated.

Forgetting information and updating it regularly is a known issue with RAG systems; however, this project ages slowly since writing and style guides change only at the pace of natural language.

3 Data

The knowledge base comprises 12 PDF documents, a total of 17 MB, drawn from three categories: essay writing guides, fiction writing guides, and test materials. All sources are publicly available resources from academic institutions and educational platforms, written predominantly in UK English. No personally identifiable information is present in any document. Table 1 provides a full overview.

Essay-writing sources cover argument structure, essay structure, vocabulary, and clarity. Fiction-writing sources address narrative style, point of view, dialogue formatting, and idiomatic language. Test materials consist of Cambridge English sample responses across CEFR levels A1–C2, an accompanying assessment guide, and an excerpt from Chapter 1 of The Fellowship of the Ring, used solely for fiction evaluation.

"""

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that injects targeted context at query time. For this purpose, the user prompt must be encoded so that a similarity search can be performed on a vector database consisting of external files. These files are predominantly used to build a knowledge-base backend to supplement compressed LLMs by retrieving task-specific information. [4]

Since the context is selected from previously prepared documents, the accuracy of responses can be greatly enhanced. This allows even compact models to achieve significantly better results if the task is specific enough and the documents are not yet outdated.

Forgetting information and updating it regularly is a known issue with RAG systems; however, this project ages slowly since writing and style guides change only at the pace of natural language.
